claims.claim: A potentially traumatic event is an exposure, not a diagnosis; most exposed people do not develop PTSD even though distress is common after serious events.
Post-event reactions vary substantially over time, and natural recovery, persistent difficulties and relatively stable functioning can all occur in trauma-exposed groups.
PTSD assessment depends on defined symptoms, duration, impairment and context; casual observations such as silence, anger or vigilance cannot establish a trauma history or diagnosis.
Violence-related burden can include ongoing threat, loss of control and social or material consequences, so analysis must distinguish an ended event from continuing exposure.
Research on continuing violence after separation shows that formal relationship termination does not necessarily end coercive or harmful dynamics and their health burden.
Behavioural signs alone are non-specific and must not be used to invent undocumented violence or trauma histories for named people.
Safety after crisis includes physical protection as well as access to information, basic needs, social support and predictable services; these conditions can shape distress and trust.

Psychological first aid is humane, supportive and practical assistance that includes listening without pressure, assessing needs and mobilising practical and social support; it is not equivalent to psychotherapy.
In the early Utøya follow-up, most interviewed survivors reported proactive outreach and many received health services, while an important minority reported unmet service needs.
Grief is a common response to bereavement with cognitive, emotional and behavioural variation across people and cultures, and most bereaved people do not follow one mandatory stage sequence.

Prolonged grief disorder affects a minority after many natural losses, while meta-analytic estimates are substantially higher after unnatural or violent losses and remain heterogeneous across studies.
Grief-related distress and posttraumatic reactions can coexist after traumatic loss but represent distinguishable processes and should not be collapsed into one label.
Collective crises can disrupt families, livelihoods, social networks and essential services at the same time as they affect individual mental health, requiring analysis across multiple levels.
The NKVTS Utøya study documents both persistent difficulties and substantial variation in reactions, social support and service use across repeated interview rounds.

The 22 July Centre is a national memorial and learning centre with an official mandate to document, teach and facilitate reflection about the 2011 attacks; its role is educational and memorial, not clinical assessment of visitors.
International emergency guidance recommends layered mental health and psychosocial support ranging from basic safety and community support to focused and specialised care according to need.
Proactive outreach after disaster can reach many affected people while still leaving unmet needs, so service quality requires attention to coverage, continuity, relevance and referral pathways.
Care systems shape access through categories, priorities and resources, which means the existence of a service must be distinguished from actual access and user experience.
Risk and protective factors are probabilistic group-level associations and cannot by themselves determine an individual person's future course or support needs.
A large meta-analysis found a robust association between greater self-reported social support and lower PTSD symptom severity, with meaningful variation across studies and moderators.

Emergency-related poverty, discrimination, family separation, reduced safety, disrupted social networks and service interruptions can add to psychological burden and must be analysed as context rather than individual weakness.
Contemporary resilience research treats resilience as dynamic adaptation shaped by multiple modifiable resources rather than a simple fixed trait or invulnerability.
Research on collective trauma identifies intrapersonal, relational or multisystemic, and sociocultural resilience frameworks, supporting analysis beyond the individual level.
Social support and other external resources can form part of resilient adaptation, so receiving help is not evidence that a person lacks resilience.
Separating documented event, reaction, time, context, support and service system prevents psychological theory from filling gaps in biographical or clinical evidence.

The 22 July Centre, NKVTS longitudinal studies and a psychology research institution answer different questions—public memory, group-level outcomes and research method—and should not be treated as interchangeable evidence about individuals.

Safe trauma and resilience education must stop before exposure becomes diagnosis, group risk becomes individual prognosis, ordinary grief becomes disorder by default or resilience becomes a moral ranking of people.
